title: Stacks and Queues
summary: This unit introduces abstract data types (abstrakte Datentypen, ADTs), information hiding (Information Hiding), stacks (Stacks), and queues (Queues). You will practice linked and array-based implementations, circular arrays, postfix evaluation, and amortized analysis (amortisierte Analyse). You will also learn how a private representation can be replaced without changing the behavior seen by the client.
keyFacts: An ADT specifies which operations are available and what they do, not how the data is stored.
A private representation protects data-structure invariants; clients use the public operations.
A stack follows LIFO: the value stored most recently is removed first.
In a linked stack, top points to the next node that pop removes.
In an array-based stack, the occupied values are in a[0] through a[size - 1]; top is at size - 1.
Before inserting into a full array, it is replaced with one twice as large.
An array is halved only when it is at most one-quarter full; the minimum capacity is 4.
For n pushes and pops starting from empty, at most 2n values are copied during resizes in total.
A single array operation can cost O(n), even though the amortized cost per operation is O(1).
Postfix notation places each operator after its two operands and is evaluated from left to right.
For noncommutative postfix operations, the right operand is popped from the stack first.
Arrow-style switch syntax has no fall-through; classic syntax requires break to prevent fall-through.
A queue follows FIFO: the value that has been waiting the longest is removed first.
A linked queue uses first and last; when removing the last element, both must become null.
A circular array queue computes indices modulo the array length and uses size to distinguish full from empty.
When an array queue is resized, its elements are copied to the beginning of the new array in logical order; afterward, first = 0.
Stack and queue ADTs can change their internal representation without requiring the client to change its calls.

review.notes: Geprüft: 42 Fragen. Im klassischen switch-Codebeispiel fehlte die Deklaration des verwendeten Stacks; ergänzt. Rechen- und Code-Ausgaben stimmen, Mermaid-Kontexte sind klein und enthalten die nötigen Daten.

questions.prompt: Which description applies to an abstract data type (ADT)?

options.text: It specifies the available operations and their behavior, but not the internal storage.
It specifies the concrete memory locations but leaves the operations open.
It describes only a program's memory usage.
It allows clients to change internal data fields directly.

questions.explanation: An ADT describes public behavior through operations. The implementation determines the concrete representation.

questions.prompt: With information hiding, the representation data remains private, so clients cannot change it directly.
questions.explanation: Private data is changed only through the data structure's methods. This allows those methods to preserve its invariants.

questions.prompt: Which statements about a stack are correct? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: push and pop operate on top.
The first value inserted is always the first one removed.
The last value inserted is removed first.
Calling pop on an empty stack is an error.

questions.explanation: A stack is LIFO: the most recently added value is on top and is removed first. An empty stack has no value to return from pop.

questions.prompt: In a stack, the most recently stored value is removed ___.
questions.explanation: LIFO means “last in, first out”: the most recently stored value is removed first.

questions.prompt: What does FIFO mean for a queue?

options.text: Values are always removed in ascending order.
Insertion and removal take place at the same end.
The value that has been waiting the longest is removed first.
The most recently inserted value is removed first.

questions.explanation: FIFO means “first in, first out”: the oldest value is removed first. Values are inserted at the back and removed from the front.

questions.prompt: What role does the private data play in the ADT shown?

context.content:
flowchart LR
  C[Client] --> P[public operations]
  P --> D[private data]
context.caption: Public operations mediate between the client and the private representation.

options.text: It is the internal representation, which the client accesses only through public operations.
It shows that every operation must use an array.
It replaces the client and calls its methods.
It is a second set of public operations for the client.

questions.explanation: The client calls public operations. These work internally with private data whose concrete form remains hidden.

questions.prompt: An array-based stack has `size = 3`. At which index is its top stored value?
questions.explanation: The occupied cells run from 0 to size - 1. Therefore, when size = 3, top is at index 2.

questions.prompt: For this array-based stack implementation, after a `pop()`, the reduced `size` is checked. If the capacity is greater than 4 and `size <= Kapazität / 4`, the array is halved; the minimum capacity is 4. Immediately before a `pop()`, an array with capacity 16 contains 5 values. Claim: after this `pop()`, the array is reduced from 16 to 8 cells. True or false?
questions.explanation: After the `pop()`, `size = 4`. Since the capacity is 16, which is greater than 4, and $4 \le 16/4$, the array is halved to 8 cells.

questions.prompt: For a circular array queue, the insertion index is `(___ + size) % a.length`.
questions.explanation: first marks the oldest value. Together with size, modulo the array length, it gives the next free position.

source.heading: Problem: Entfernen hinterlässt freie Zellen am Anfang

questions.prompt: Which statements about a circular array queue are correct? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: `first` alone always distinguishes a full queue from an empty one.
`size == a.length` means the queue is full.
When the array is resized, values are copied in logical order and `first` is then set to 0.

questions.explanation: size distinguishes empty from full. When resized, the logical queue is laid out starting at index 0 in the new array.

questions.prompt: Where does an operator appear in postfix notation?
questions.explanation: In postfix notation, the two operands come first and the operator follows them, as in `3 5 +`.
The first two pops return right = 3 and left = 9, so the result is 6. This is then multiplied by 2, and 12 is output.

source.heading: Der top-Wert ist der rechte Operand

questions.prompt: Evaluate the postfix expression `8 3 -`. For `-`, the right operand is popped first, then the left.
questions.explanation: 3 is on top, so right = 3; then left = 8 is popped. This gives 8 − 3 = 5.

source.heading: Der top-Wert ist der rechte Operand

questions.prompt: A stack is initially empty. Perform `push(2)`, `push(7)`, `pop()`, `push(4)`, `pop()`, `pop()`. What value does the third `pop()` return?

options.text: The stack is then empty and returns no value.

questions.explanation: The pops return 7, 4, and 2, in that order. The oldest value remains at the bottom of the stack until the last pop.

questions.prompt: A circular queue reads its logical values starting at `first` and then continues modulo the array length. Which value is removed next?

context.caption: The queue is full; its logical order starts at `first = 2`.

questions.explanation: `first` points to index 2. It contains the oldest value, 3, so that is the next value returned by dequeue.
First, 3 · 2 = 6. Then 9 − 6 is calculated, giving 3.

questions.prompt: A linked queue is empty. What must `first` and `last` refer to after `enqueue(7)`?

options.text: Both remain `null` until a second value is inserted.
Both point to the same new node, which contains the value 7.
`first` points to the new node, while `last` remains `null`.
`last` points to the new node, while `first` remains `null`.

questions.explanation: When a value is inserted into an empty queue, the new node is both the first and the last node.

source.heading: enqueue: neuen Knoten hinter den letzten hängen

questions.prompt: In an array-based stack, `push(x)` first writes the new value at index `___` and then increments `size`.
questions.explanation: size is the index of the first free cell. After writing the value, size is incremented by one.

source.heading: push in die erste freie Zelle

questions.prompt: An array-based stack has capacity 8 and contains 3 values before a `pop()`. For this implementation, after the removal, the new `size` is checked. If the capacity is greater than 4 and `size <= Kapazität / 4`, the capacity is halved. The minimum capacity is 4; when resizing, only the remaining values are copied. Which statements apply to this `pop()`? Select all that apply.

options.text: After the `pop()`, 2 values remain; the array is reduced from 8 to 4 cells.
The capacity may fall below 4 when the array shrinks.
The shrinking test uses `size` after the removal.
When resizing, all 8 cells are copied, including the unused ones.

questions.explanation: After the `pop()`, `size = 2`, so $2 \le 8/4$ holds and the capacity is halved to 4. Only the 2 remaining values are copied. The test uses the reduced `size`; the minimum capacity prevents shrinking below 4.

questions.prompt: A circular array queue has an array length of 4 and `first = 3`. After a dequeue, `first` is set to `(first + 1) % a.length`. What value does it receive?
questions.explanation: (3 + 1) % 4 = 0. At the end of the array, the front index wraps around to index 0.
The `+` case pushes 8. Without `break`, execution also enters the `*` case, which puts 15 on top of the stack.

questions.prompt: For `a = [5, 6, 3, 4]`, `first = 2`, and `size = 4`, the logical order of the queue is `[3, 4, 5, 6]`.
questions.explanation: The values are read starting at index 2, then continue with wrap-around at index 0: 3, 4, 5, 6.

questions.prompt: Which statements explain the benefits of an ADT with a private representation? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: The methods can protect the data structure's rules.
The same set of operations can be implemented using different representations.
The client uses the public operations.
The client can change private fields directly.

questions.explanation: An ADT hides its representation from the client. Its own methods control changes and can enforce invariants.

questions.prompt: Each group ends with a resize; the tail that follows contains none. What bound on the total number of copies follows from the grouping shown?

context.content:
flowchart LR
  G1["Group 1: n₁ ops, ≤ 2n₁ copies, resize"] --> G2["Group 2: n₂ ops, ≤ 2n₂ copies, resize"] --> GK["Group k: nₖ ops, ≤ 2nₖ copies, resize"] --> T["Tail: no resize, 0 copies"]
context.caption: Each group ends with a resize; the tail does not.

options.text: The tail always copies as many values as the last group.

questions.explanation: Each group with nᵢ operations causes at most 2nᵢ copies; the tail causes none. Together, the groups contain at most n operations.

questions.prompt: A linked queue contains exactly one node. `dequeue()` removes it and sets `first` to `null`. What additional update is needed?

options.text: Reset `last` to point to the removed node.
Set `first` to point to the removed node again.
Add one more node to the queue.

questions.explanation: After removing the last element, the empty queue must be represented by `first == null` and `last == null`.

questions.prompt: An array-based stack starts with capacity 4 and `size = 0`. It receives five pushes and then three pops. It doubles before a push when full and halves after a pop when at most one-quarter full, but never below capacity 4. What are its final capacity and `size`?
questions.explanation: The fifth push doubles the capacity to 8. After three pops, size = 2; the quarter-full rule therefore applies and the capacity is halved to 4.

questions.prompt: When evaluating `8 3 -`, the right operand is on top. Therefore, the first value popped for subtraction is ___.
questions.explanation: The last value pushed, 3, is on top and is the right operand. Then 8 is popped as the left operand.

source.heading: Der top-Wert ist der rechte Operand

questions.prompt: An array-based stack with capacity 8 and 5 values halves on every single alternating operation `pop`, `push`, `pop`, `push` if it shrinks when half full.
questions.explanation: The first pop reduces size to 4 and halves the capacity to 4. The next push fills the array and immediately doubles it again; this repeats.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the amortized analysis of an array-based stack are correct? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: It bounds the cost of an entire sequence of operations.
A single operation can still cost O(n).
For n pushes and pops starting from empty, at most 2n resize copies are needed.
Each individual operation copies at most two values.

questions.explanation: The bound applies to the whole sequence, not to each operation individually. A resize can copy many values at once, but the total remains at most 2n.

source.heading: 35.3 Amortisierte Analyse: Wie viel wird insgesamt kopiert?

questions.prompt: A sequence of 12 pushes and pops starts with an empty stack. According to the amortized bound, what is the maximum number of resize copies?
questions.explanation: The bound is at most 2n copies. For n = 12, this gives 2 · 12 = 24.

source.heading: 35.3 Amortisierte Analyse: Wie viel wird insgesamt kopiert?

questions.prompt: A client uses only `enqueue`, `dequeue`, and `isEmpty` of a queue. When switching from a linked implementation to a circular array implementation, what can remain unchanged?

options.text: The internal fields `first` and `last` must be changed in the client.
The client must copy the values itself in physical array order.
The calls and client logic, provided the queue retains the same FIFO behavior.
The queue must make its representation public.

questions.explanation: The client depends on the ADT's behavior and its public operations, not on how the data is stored privately.

source.heading: Ein ADT erlaubt den Wechsel der Implementierung

questions.explanation: The first operator gives 4 − 2 = 2. Then 8 · 2 is calculated, giving 16.

questions.prompt: A circular queue has an array length of 8, `first = 6`, and `size = 4`. At which physical index is the value at logical position `i = 2`? Use `(first + i) % a.length`.
questions.explanation: (6 + 2) % 8 = 0. Because of wrap-around, the third logical value is in array cell 0.
`b = a` does not create a second stack. `b.push(9)` modifies the same stack object, so 9 is on top and is removed by `a.pop()`.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the postfix expression `9 5 3 - * 2 +`. Each operator combines the top two stack values; for `-`, the pop order matters.
questions.explanation: 5 − 3 gives 2, then 9 · 2 = 18, and finally 18 + 2 = 20.

questions.prompt: A circular queue has capacity 4, `first = 2`, and the logical sequence `[7, 8, 9]`. The physical cells contain `a[2]=7`, `a[3]=8`, and `a[0]=9`; `a[1]` is empty. Perform `enqueue(10)`, `enqueue(11)`, and `dequeue()`. What are the final values of front, size, and capacity? When the array is full, it doubles; resizing copies values in logical order.
questions.explanation: `enqueue(10)` fills the fourth cell. The next enqueue triggers a resize, resulting in `[7,8,9,10,11]` with first = 0. The dequeue removes 7; afterward, 8 is at the front, size = 4, and the capacity remains 8.

questions.prompt: A queue can be implemented with linked nodes or as a circular array. Linked insertions link a node without traversing the queue; array cells are adjacent, but a full array must be copied when it grows. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: The linked implementation avoids a large copy for a single insertion.
With doubling and shrinking at one-quarter full, array operations are amortized O(1).
The linked implementation uses less memory per value than an int in a shared array.
The array implementation stores values in adjacent cells.

questions.explanation: Linked nodes avoid copying the entire queue on insertion. Arrays provide adjacent cells and amortized O(1) operations, but resizing requires copying to a larger array.

questions.prompt: A client could change `top` of a stack directly and bypass the LIFO rule. Which design protects the stack invariant?

options.text: Sort every stack value on every method call.
Keep `top` private and allow changes only through `push` and `pop`.
Make `top` public and ask clients to be careful.
Remove the stack operations and make only `toString()` public.

questions.explanation: Private representation data can be changed only through stack methods. This allows those methods to preserve the structure's rules.

questions.prompt: With recursive methods, the most recently started call returns first. This corresponds to the LIFO principle of a stack.
questions.explanation: Each recursive call places a stack frame on the stack. The frames are processed in the reverse order of the calls.

questions.prompt: A linked queue contains the nodes `A → B → C → null`, where `first` points to A. `dequeue()` reads the value at first and updates `first = first.next`. What contents and reference remain afterward?

options.text: A → C remain; `first` points to A.
B → C remain; `first` points to B.
Only C remains; `first` points to C.

questions.explanation: `dequeue()` removes the first node by setting first to its successor. The links from B to C remain unchanged.

questions.prompt: A postfix calculator processes `8 3 -`. Which statements correctly describe the evaluation? Select all that apply; more than one may be correct.

options.text: In classic `case '-' :` syntax, a missing `break` can cause fall-through.
Arrow syntax `case '-' ->` does not continue into the next case.
For subtraction, the right operand, 3, is on top of the stack.
8 is popped first and used as the right operand.

questions.explanation: The tokens are processed from left to right, so 3 is on top. Arrow syntax prevents fall-through; classic syntax requires a break for that.
The stack returns 7, and the queue returns 4. The difference is 7 − 4 = 3.

questions.prompt: In a circular array queue, the next insertion index can point to `first` when the queue is either empty or full. `size` distinguishes these states.
questions.explanation: Because of wrap-around, the insertion index returns to first. `size == 0` indicates empty, and `size == a.length` indicates full.

questions.prompt: You click “Undo” in a text editor: the most recent change should be undone first. Which data structure fits this behavior?
questions.explanation: A stack removes the most recently added values first (LIFO). This lets an editor undo the most recent change first.

questions.prompt: Your messaging app queues outgoing messages when service is interrupted. The app should process them in the order they arrived, with the oldest message first. Which data structure fits?
questions.explanation: A queue follows FIFO: the message that has been waiting the longest is removed first. This matches the required arrival order.

questions.prompt: You push 13 values onto an array-based stack with an initial capacity of 4. If the array is full, its capacity is doubled before the next `push`. How many resizes occur?
questions.explanation: The capacity grows from 4 to 8 before the fifth value is inserted, and from 8 to 16 before the ninth. There is enough room for the remaining pushes, so there are 2 resizes.

questions.prompt: You enter `8 3 -` into a simple postfix calculator. It reads from left to right, pushes numbers onto a stack, and for `-` computes `links - rechts` first (the right operand is popped first). What result is displayed?
questions.explanation: The calculator pushes 8 and then 3 onto the stack. It takes 3 as the right operand and 8 as the left operand, and calculates $8-3=5$.

source.heading: Der top-Wert ist der rechte Operand

questions.prompt: Your team changes a queue library internally: it now uses a circular array instead of linked nodes. If its public methods `enqueue` and `dequeue` still provide the same FIFO behavior, does the client need to change its calls?
questions.explanation: An ADT describes the public operations and their behavior, not the storage. If this contract stays the same, the private representation can change without requiring the client to update its calls.

source.heading: Ein ADT erlaubt den Wechsel der Implementierung

questions.prompt: An array queue starts empty. For any 100 valid `enqueue` and `dequeue` operations, amortized analysis guarantees at most $2n$ resize copies for $n$ operations. What is this upper bound on the number of copied values for $n=100$?
questions.explanation: The bound given in the prompt is $2n$. With $n=100$, this gives $2\cdot100=200$ copied values; a particular sequence may require fewer copies.

questions.prompt: A library provides a queue with `enqueue` and `dequeue`. Its internal fields `first` and `last` are private. What is the main reason for this?

options.text: So the queue always outputs its elements in sorted order.
So clients cannot violate the queue's state rules by changing its fields directly.
So clients cannot call any of the public queue methods.

questions.explanation: Private fields protect the representation. This lets the queue preserve its invariants through its own methods, such as `first` and `last` for an empty queue.

questions.prompt: A circular array has capacity 7. `first = 5` and `size = 4`. The insertion index is `(first + size) mod Kapazität`. At which array index will the next value be placed?
questions.explanation: Substituting into the formula gives $(5+4)\bmod7=9\bmod7=2$. The next value will therefore be placed at index 2.

questions.prompt: You are programming a ring-buffer queue with capacity $C$; its insertion index is `(first + size) mod C`. This index can point to `first` when the queue is empty or full. Is it true that `size` distinguishes the two cases: empty when `0`, full when `C`?
questions.explanation: Yes. The index alone does not distinguish empty from full, but `size` does: `0` means empty, and `C` means all cells are occupied.

questions.prompt: You implement operator selection in a Java postfix calculator using `switch`. The team requires that a selected operator execute exactly one branch, even if someone does not add a `break`. The Java version in use supports arrow syntax in `switch`. Which form directly meets this requirement?

options.text: Multiple classic `case` labels before the same statement

questions.explanation: With arrow syntax, only the selected branch runs; there is no fall-through. In classic syntax, a `break` is needed to prevent execution from continuing into the next case.
